abstract: While most research on AI's labor market impact focuses on occupational exposure, this analysis reveals that adaptive capacity—workers' ability to manage job transitions—varies significantly. Of 37.1 million workers in the top quartile of AI exposure, 26.5 million possess above-median adaptive capacity and are well-positioned to weather job displacement. However, 6.1 million workers (4.2% of the workforce) face high AI exposure combined with low adaptive capacity, concentrated in clerical and administrative roles and disproportionately women (86%), primarily in smaller metros and college towns.
keyFindings: Of 37.1 million highly AI-exposed workers, 26.5 million have above-median adaptive capacity and are positioned to manage job transitions successfully.
6.1 million workers (4.2% of the workforce) face both high AI exposure and low adaptive capacity, with 86% being women, concentrated in clerical and administrative occupations.
A positive correlation exists between AI exposure and adaptive capacity, meaning highly exposed workers in managerial and technical roles are more financially secure and better networked.
Office clerks (2.5 million), secretaries and administrative assistants (1.7 million), receptionists (965,000), and medical secretaries (831,000) represent the largest vulnerable occupations.

Vulnerable workers are geographically concentrated in smaller metro areas, college towns, and state capitals, particularly in the Mountain West and Midwest, ranging from 2.4% to 6.9% of metro employment.
methodology: The study combines six primary datasets: Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) 2022-2024 for liquid wealth data; American Community Survey (ACS) 2024 for age distributions; Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) 2024 for wage and employment figures; Bureau of Labor Statistics employment projections (2024-2034) for growth rates; Lightcast 2023 for county and metro employment data; and O*NET Database 30.1 (2025) for skill importance ratings. AI exposure measures derive from Eloundou et al. (2024). The analysis creates a composite occupation-level adaptive capacity index based on four standardized components: net liquid wealth, growth-weighted skill transferability, geographic density, and age. The final dataset covers 95.9% of the U.S. workforce across 356 occupations, with only occupations meeting strict data quality thresholds (≥15 SIPP respondents) included.
qualifiers: The adaptive capacity index is computed at the occupation level, but individual workers within the same occupation can vary substantially in adaptive capacity. The index represents an initial attempt at measuring this concept and captures factors influencing job-finding and post-displacement earnings but not the full range of welfare costs from job loss. Evidence is derived primarily from localized displacement events rather than large-scale occupational shifts, so it may be most informative for isolated job losses rather than simultaneous cluster displacement. If AI creates structural changes comparable to the industrial revolution or simultaneously affects clusters of related occupations, skill availability and other dynamics could render the measure less applicable. Significant uncertainty remains about the extent to which AI will impact labor markets and differential outcomes for affected workers.
